body:
Last night on 
Predictable
, we got another perfect example of how the media covers prediction markets.
And by “covers,” I mean wildly overreacts to them while completely ignoring much larger and more obvious corruption happening right in front of their faces.
The latest panic came courtesy of an NPR story about campaign staffers allegedly using insider information to make money on election prediction markets. Judging by the reaction online, you’d think they uncovered the largest financial scandal in American history.
What Did They Actually Find?
One anonymous guy.
That’s basically the story.
One unnamed campaign staffer claimed he got access to an unreleased poll, bought shares before the information became public, and made a few thousand dollars after the market moved.
Now, let me be clear about this:
If that happened, it’s insider trading.
It’s illegal.
These markets are regulated.
The exchanges don’t want it happening.
The CFTC doesn’t want it happening either.
And if regulators can identify the people doing it, they can absolutely face consequences for it.
But the scale of the outrage compared to the scale of the offense is what makes this whole thing ridiculous.
The Part Nobody in DC Wants To Talk About
Washington barely blinks when billions disappear into government waste projects.
Nobody seems all that interested when politicians somehow post stock market returns that would make hedge fund managers jealous.
Nancy Pelosi’s investment track record apparently raises fewer eyebrows than one campaign staffer allegedly making a few thousand dollars off a poll release.
That’s the part that’s hard to take seriously.
And honestly, part of the reason prediction markets make people uncomfortable is because they often get to the truth faster than the media does.
That’s what markets are designed to do.
They absorb information quickly. They react to reality quickly. Sometimes 
too
 quickly for the comfort of people who are used to controlling narratives for a living.
Why Prediction Markets Matter
We talked about the Los Angeles mayoral race as an example.
Before the polling shifted, before the donor panic, before the media consensus changed, the markets immediately reacted to a disastrous debate performance and quantified what everyone watching already knew.
That’s valuable.
It doesn’t mean markets are perfect. They aren’t.
There are:
bad actors
manipulators
insiders
people trying to game systems
Welcome to literally every financial market on earth.
Part of participating in prediction markets is understanding uncertainty itself is part of the investment.
You are never entering a market with perfect information. Neither am I. Neither is anybody else. That uncertainty is part of the price.
One Of The Biggest Mistakes New Traders Make
We also spent a good chunk of the episode answering questions from newer viewers, because I realize a lot of people coming into this world are still trying to understand the basics.
One of the biggest concepts people struggle with is the difference between being 
right
 and finding 
value.
Those are not the same thing.
You can correctly predict an outcome and still make a terrible investment if:
the upside is too small
the time horizon is too long
the risk isn’t worth it
That’s why I keep hammering APY and time horizon over and over again.
A three-year position with limited upside might not actually be very attractive even if you think the outcome is likely.
That’s also why I focus so much on stacking smaller gains over time instead of chasing giant lottery-ticket outcomes.
We’re trying to build sustainable edges here.
Not dopamine addictions.
Also…
We spent some time mocking politicians who want to ban activities that are already illegal because apparently nobody in Washington actually understands how these markets work.
Shocking development, I know.
